summary: The article provides a largely accurate overview of Fixed Deposit taxation in India, including TDS rules, Form 15G/15H, and tax-saving FDs. However, some TDS thresholds are outdated for the current financial year (FY 2025-26).

claims.claim: Interest earned on a Fixed Deposit is classified under the head 'Income from Other Sources' as per the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm this classification under Section 56(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

claims.claim: Banks deduct Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) if your FD interest exceeds ₹40,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizens) in a financial year.
claims.note: For FY 2025-26, the TDS threshold for non-senior citizens is ₹50,000 and for senior citizens is ₹1,00,000. The article's figures are for FY 2024-25.

claims.claim: If you have not provided your PAN, the TDS rate jumps to 20%.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm a 20% TDS rate if PAN is not provided.

claims.claim: You can submit Form 15G (for non-senior citizens) or Form 15H (for senior citizens) to avoid TDS if your total income is below the taxable limit.
claims.note: Forms 15G and 15H are indeed used for this purpose, with specific eligibility criteria for age and income.

claims.claim: Tax-Saving FDs come with a mandatory lock-in period of 5 years.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm the 5-year lock-in period for tax-saving FDs.

claims.claim: The principal amount invested in these FDs, up to a maximum of ₹1.5 lakhs in a financial year, is eligible for deduction under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: This is a core feature of tax-saving FDs under Section 80C.

claims.claim: For cumulative FDs, the interest is taxable on an accrual basis each financial year, even if you don't physically receive it until maturity.
claims.note: Several sources confirm that interest on cumulative FDs is taxable on an accrual basis annually.

article_title: Fixed Deposits: Tax on FD Interest & Key Rules for Depositors
